name: Hair-growth inhibitor lotion

lead: These lotions aim to slow how fast unwanted facial or body hair comes back, so smooth skin lasts longer between shaves. The prescription version, eflornithine cream, is used for facial hair in women and has clinical data behind it.

Eflornithine blocks an enzyme (ornithine decarboxylase) in the follicle, which slows hair growth rather than removing hair. Wikipedia reports that in clinical studies 81% of women showed improvement after twelve months, with the effect beginning around eight weeks. Over-the-counter retardant lotions vary in ingredients and no trials of them were found.

paras: People apply the lotion to the area after shaving, waxing or plucking, alongside their normal hair removal routine. The effect is gradual, and removal methods continue to be used.
Acne, stinging, itching and rash are reported with eflornithine. Hair regrows to baseline within about eight weeks of stopping. It is a prescription product.

angle.text: Inhibitor lotions slow follicle regrowth so smooth skin lasts longer between shaves or waxes. The prescription ingredient eflornithine has trial data for facial hair in women; over-the-counter versions vary.

lead: Hair-growth inhibitor lotions are topical products marketed to slow the regrowth of unwanted body or facial hair, usually after shaving, waxing or plucking. The term covers both a prescription cream and over-the-counter lotions sold as retardants.

The best documented active ingredient is eflornithine, an inhibitor of the enzyme ornithine decarboxylase, sold as a prescription cream for facial hair in women [1]. Wikipedia reports that in clinical studies 81% of women showed improvement after twelve months, that the effect begins around eight weeks, and that hair returns to baseline within about eight weeks of stopping [1]. Evidence for over-the-counter retardant lotions is not available in the sources reviewed.

paras: Eflornithine acts as an irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase, an enzyme involved in cell growth in the hair follicle [1]. It is described as the only prescription topical treatment that slows facial hair growth and as reducing the psychological burden of facial hirsutism [1]. Acne is the most common side effect (7 to 14%), with itching, redness, stinging, dryness and rash also reported [1].

Non-prescription products sold as hair retardants are generally used as an adjunct to shaving or waxing. No clinical trials of these formulations were identified for this article, and the active ingredients vary by brand.
No studies found for over-the-counter hair-growth inhibitor lotions. For the prescription ingredient eflornithine, the clinical results are summarized above [1].
